summary: Generics (Java 5) turn runtime ClassCastExceptions into compile-time errors and remove casts. The diamond `<>` came in Java 7.
Generics exist only at compile time (type erasure). Wildcards: `<?>` any type, `<? extends T>` T or its subtypes (read), `<? super T>` T or its supertypes (write).

There are 4 ways to traverse a collection: index for loop, for-each, Iterator (the only safe way to remove), and stream forEach. Removing through the list inside a loop throws ConcurrentModificationException.
Java 8: lambdas implement a functional interface (exactly one abstract method). Method references (5 kinds). Streams: source, lazy intermediate ops, then one terminal op.

Java 8 interfaces can have default methods (with a body, can be overridden) and static methods (cannot be overridden). A conflict between two defaults must be resolved by overriding, optionally calling `X.super.m()`.
Enhanced switch ('Java 12+'): arrow cases with no fall-through, multiple labels per case, switch as an expression, and `yield` to return a value from a block.
mustMemorise: Versions per slides: Java 5 = Generics, Collections enhancements, Enhanced for. Java 7 = diamond <>. Java 8 = Lambdas, Streams, Default methods. Java 12+ = Enhanced switch
Raw type + wrong cast = ClassCastException at RUNTIME. With generics, a wrong add = COMPILE-TIME error

Type erasure: type arguments are removed after compilation, so List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class at runtime. No `new T()`, no `instanceof T`, no `List<int>`, no overloads that differ only by type argument

`? extends Fruit` = Fruit and subclasses (upper bound): you can READ Fruit out but can't add. `? super Fruit` = Fruit and superclasses (lower bound): you can ADD Fruit or Apple, and get() returns Object
Naming: E Element, K Key, V Value, N Number, T Type, S/U/V = 2nd/3rd/4th type
Collection extends Iterable. Map is NOT a Collection
Remove during iteration: only `iterator.remove()` is safe. `list.remove()` inside a for-each or iterator loop gives ConcurrentModificationException
Lambda syntax: (arguments) -> { body }. It needs a functional interface = exactly ONE abstract method
5 method-reference kinds: Static (Integer::parseInt), Bound (obj::m), Unbound (String::toLowerCase), Class constructor (TreeMap::new), Array constructor (int[]::new)
Streams: intermediate ops (filter, map, sorted, distinct) return a Stream and are lazy. Terminal ops (collect, forEach) produce a result. Streams don't store or modify the source
Two interfaces with the same default method gives a compile error unless the class overrides it. Pick one with `A.super.show()`
Default method: can be overridden. Static interface method: cannot be overridden; call it as `Utility.m()`. Abstract method: must be implemented
Enhanced switch: `case 'A', 'B' -> 100;`, no fall-through, `int x = switch(...) {...};` ends with `;`, and `yield v;` returns from a block

items.title: Evolution of Java
notes: Order: Java 1.x, then Java 5, then Java 8, then Java 12+.
Java 5 (= 1.5) brought big language changes (generics, for-each). Java 7, 8, 9 broadened what Java could do.
Map each feature to its version; see slide 60.

items.title: Before generics: raw type, runtime ClassCastException
notes: A raw `List` accepts anything: `add("Java")` and `add(2)` both compile.
`(String) myList.get(1)` **compiles** but throws `ClassCastException: Integer cannot be cast to String` at **runtime**.
The slide's comment puts the error on the println line. In real Java it is thrown **at the cast line**, so the next println never runs (verified). Exam: the answer is 'compiles, CCE at runtime'.

items.title: With generics: compile-time error
notes: `List<String>`: `myList.add(2)` is a **compile-time error** ('int cannot be converted to String'). Generics move the error from runtime to compile time.
`String str = myList.get(0);` needs **no cast**.

Slide bug: the lines under `add(2)` were copied from slide 5. Because `add(2)` fails, the program doesn't compile at all, so it cannot 'throw CCE at runtime'. Without `add(2)`, `get(1)` would throw IndexOutOfBoundsException.

items.title: ArrayList UML before and after JDK 1.5
notes: Before 1.5 the API used `Object`. Since 1.5, `ArrayList<E>` uses `add(o: E)`, `get(index): E`, `set(index, o: E): E`.
Methods like `contains(o: Object)`, `indexOf(Object)` and `remove(o: Object)` **stay Object** even in the generic version.

Slide inaccuracy (from the textbook figure): the real `add(E)` returns **boolean**, not void, and `remove(int index)` returns the **removed element (E)**, not boolean. If asked about the real API, use the real types.

items.title: Generic class definition, and type erasure
notes: `class ArrayList<E>`: E is a **type parameter**, used in `add(E element)`.
The backing store is `Object[] elements`. That is **type erasure**: after compilation, E becomes Object and the compiler inserts casts.
Erasure means `new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass()` is **true** (verified). Erasure is not stated on the slides, but it is a weak point.
Simplified: the real ArrayList extends AbstractList and implements List, RandomAccess and others.

items.title: Diamond operator: Java 7
notes: Before Java 7: `new ArrayList<String>()`, with the type written on both sides.
Java 7+: `new ArrayList<>()`. The type is **inferred** on the right-hand side.
Trap: the diamond is Java **7**, not Java 5 (generics) or Java 8.

items.title: Custom generic class Box<T>
notes: `Box<Integer> intBox = new Box<>(); intBox.set(123); Integer number = intBox.get();` needs no cast. 123 is autoboxed to Integer.
Type arguments must be **reference types**: `Box<int>` is a compile error.
Erasure rules: inside Box you **cannot** write `new T()` or `x instanceof T` (both are compile errors, verified).

items.title: Multiple type parameters Box<T, U>
notes: `Box<String, Double> priceBox = new Box<>("Laptop", 799.99);`
Output: `Item: Laptop, Price: $799.99`.
This slide uses U as the 2nd parameter, while slide 14's convention calls U the 3rd. Names are only conventions; the compiler doesn't care.

items.title: Bounded wildcards: extends vs super
notes: Green = types allowed. `List<? extends Fruit>` (**upper bounded**) accepts List<Fruit>, List<Apple>, List<Banana>, but **not** List<Food>.
`List<? super Fruit>` (**lower bounded**) accepts List<Fruit>, List<Food> (and List<Object>), but **not** List<Apple>.

Use: with `? extends`, you can **read** elements as Fruit but **cannot add** (compile error, verified). With `? super`, you can **add** a Fruit or Apple, but `get()` only gives Object (verified). PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

Trap: the arrows here point parent to child (Food→Fruit), the opposite of UML generalisation arrows. Also, `List<Fruit> l = new ArrayList<Apple>();` does NOT compile, because generics are not covariant.

items.title: Unbounded wildcard <?>
notes: Use `<?>` when you don't know or care about the type. `printList(List<?> list)` works for both List<String> and List<Integer>.
Elements are read as `Object` (`for (Object element : list)`).
You can't add anything (except null) to a `List<?>`.

items.title: Type parameter naming conventions
notes: **E** Element (collections), **K** Key, **V** Value (maps), **N** Number, **T** Type (first type param).
**S, U, V** = 2nd, 3rd, 4th type parameters. V appears twice on the slide (Value *and* 4th type), as in Oracle's tutorial.
These are conventions only, not enforced by the compiler.

items.title: Collections Framework hierarchy
notes: Green = interface, orange = class. A solid arrow means **extends**, a dotted arrow means **implements**.
Iterable ← Collection ← List / Queue / Set. Queue ← Deque. Set ← SortedSet ← TreeSet.

List classes: ArrayList, LinkedList, Vector (Stack extends Vector). LinkedList also implements **Deque**. ArrayDeque implements Deque. PriorityQueue implements Queue. HashSet and LinkedHashSet implement Set.

**Map is separate, not a Collection** (circled). HashMap, LinkedHashMap and Hashtable implement Map. TreeMap implements SortedMap. The figure simplifies a little: LinkedHashMap actually extends HashMap and LinkedHashSet extends HashSet.

items.title: 4 ways to traverse a collection
notes: **Basic for** suits index access. **Enhanced for-each** is simple, but no modifications. **Iterator** is flexible and allows **safe removal**. **Stream forEach()** is the functional approach.
'No modifications' in a for-each means no **structural** change: calling `list.remove` or `list.add` inside it gives ConcurrentModificationException (verified for add and remove).
Reassigning the loop variable (`fruit = ...`) compiles but does not change the list.

items.title: Enhanced for-each syntax
notes: `for (Type variable : collection) { ... }` works on **arrays** and any **Iterable** collection.
Type = element type. variable = the current element. collection = the array or collection.
There is no index available. Use a basic for if you need `i`.

items.title: Iterator and ConcurrentModificationException
notes: Rule: **always use `iterator.remove()`** to delete during iteration. `list.remove()` inside the loop leads to **ConcurrentModificationException**.
Pattern: `while (it.hasNext()) { String f = it.next(); if (...) it.remove(); }`. Call `next()` before `remove()`.

Real-Java catch: if `list` is the `Arrays.asList(...)` list from the previous slides, `iterator.remove()` throws **UnsupportedOperationException**, because that list is fixed-size (verified). It works on a `new ArrayList<>(...)`.
Edge case: removing the second-to-last element via `list.remove` happens not to throw (verified), but the exam answer is CME.

items.title: Stream forEach with a lambda
notes: `list.stream().forEach(item -> System.out.println("Element: " + item));`
`.stream()` creates a stream, `.forEach()` visits each element, and the lambda prints it.

items.title: Anonymous class: before lambdas
notes: `Greeting greeting = new Greeting() { public void sayHello() {...} };` creates an unnamed class implementing the interface. Note the `;` after the closing brace.
The implementing method must be `public`, because interface methods are implicitly public.
Slide 24 shows the traditional way, a named class with a method. Slide 26 shows the same thing as a lambda.

items.title: Lambda basic syntax
notes: `(arguments) -> { body }`
`Greeting greeting = () -> System.out.println("Hello, World!");` then `greeting.sayHello();` prints Hello, World!
The lambda supplies the body of the interface's single abstract method `sayHello()`.

items.title: Interface vs functional vs marker interface
notes: **Functional interface** = exactly **one abstract method** (e.g. `Runnable.run()`). `@FunctionalInterface` is optional: it just makes the compiler check.
**Marker interface** = no methods (e.g. `Serializable`).

The slide says a normal interface has 'all methods abstract'. That is the pre-Java-8 view: since Java 8 interfaces can also have default and static methods, and a functional interface may have them too.
An interface with 2 abstract methods can't be a lambda target ('not a functional interface', verified).

items.title: Lambda anatomy
notes: `(int arg1, String arg2)` is the **argument list**, `->` is the **arrow token**, and `{ ... }` is the **body**.
Explicit parameter types are allowed. If you give them, the parentheses are required.

items.title: BiConsumer example
notes: `BiConsumer<Integer, String>` has one abstract method, `void accept(T t, U u)`.
`myLambda.accept(5, "Hello");` prints `Two arguments: 5 and Hello`.
A Consumer returns nothing (void). The slide only names BiConsumer; the other standard interfaces aren't covered.

items.title: Lambda syntax variants
notes: No args: `() -> ...`. One arg: `s -> ...` (parentheses optional). Two args: `(x, y) -> x + y`.
Explicit types: `(Integer x, Integer y) -> x + y`.
Multiple statements need `{ }` and an explicit `return` if a value is returned. A single expression body has no `return` and no braces.
Not on the slide, but real Java: local variables used inside a lambda must be **effectively final** (compile error otherwise, verified).

items.title: Why use lambdas
notes: **Shorter code**: removes unnecessary method names and return keywords.
**Easier to read**: less clutter.
**Better for functional interfaces**: works well with Consumer, BiFunction, etc.

items.title: 5 kinds of method references
notes: **Static** `Integer::parseInt` = `str -> Integer.parseInt(str)`.
**Bound** `Instant.now()::isAfter`: the receiver object is fixed (evaluated once). `System.out::println` is also bound.
**Unbound** `String::toLowerCase` = `str -> str.toLowerCase()`: the first argument becomes the receiver.
**Class constructor** `TreeMap<K,V>::new` = `() -> new TreeMap<K,V>()`. **Array constructor** `int[]::new` = `len -> new int[len]`.

items.title: Lambda best practices
notes: Keep lambdas **short and focused**.
Use **method references** where possible.
Avoid heavy logic in lambda bodies.

items.title: Stream example: output [ALICE]
notes: `filter(name -> name.startsWith("A"))` keeps Alice. `.map(String::toUpperCase)` gives ALICE. `.collect(Collectors.toList())`.
Prints `[ALICE]` (verified). The original `names` list is unchanged.

items.title: Stream pipeline
notes: **Source** (array, collection, I/O), then **create stream**, then zero or more **intermediate operations** (filter, sort, map: method chaining), then **one terminal operation**, then the **result** (count, sum, a collection).
Intermediate ops return a Stream. The terminal op ends the stream. Reusing a consumed stream throws IllegalStateException (verified, not on the slide).

items.title: Key features of streams
notes: **Do not store data**. **Immutable processing**: they don't modify the source and create new results.
**Lazy evaluation**: intermediate ops run only when a terminal op is invoked (verified: nothing runs before forEach).
Intermediate = `filter()`, `map()` (return streams). Terminal = `collect()`, `forEach()` (produce results). `reduce()` is also mentioned.
`.parallelStream()` gives parallel processing. The slide says 'faster on large datasets', but it is not guaranteed faster.

items.title: Stream map / filter / sorted / collect outputs
notes: Slide 39 filter `startsWith("A")` on Alice, Bob, Charlie gives `[Alice]`.
Slide 40 `map(n -> n * n)` on 1,2,3,4 gives `[1, 4, 9, 16]`. map = **transform each element**.
Slide 41 `sorted()` = natural order: `[Alice, Bob, Charlie]`.
Slide 43 `filter(name -> name.length() > 3)` gives `[Alice, Charlie]` (Bob has 3 letters, and 3 > 3 is false).

items.title: Terminal forEach
notes: `names.stream().forEach(System.out::println);` prints Alice, Bob, Charlie on separate lines.
forEach is **terminal**: it consumes the stream. `System.out::println` is a bound method reference.

items.title: Parallel streams
notes: `numbers.parallelStream().map(n -> n * n).collect(Collectors.toList())` gives `[1, 4, 9, 16]`. collect keeps the encounter order.
`parallelStream()` is called on the collection, instead of `stream()`.

items.title: Complex chained stream
notes: filter starts-with-A, then toUpperCase, then sorted, then distinct, then collect gives `[ALICE]`.
These are all intermediate ops until `collect`, the single terminal op.

items.title: Default method definition
notes: A default method is an interface method **with a body**, declared with the `default` keyword (Java 8).
`void start();` is abstract and must be implemented. `default void stop() {...}` is inherited and can be overridden.
Interface methods are implicitly `public`, so an override in a class must also be `public`.

items.title: Why default methods
notes: Before Java 8, adding a new method to `Printer` broke **every** implementing class, which then had to implement it.
With `default void scan() {...}`, old implementers keep compiling and inherit scan(). That is **API evolution / backward compatibility**.

items.title: Default-method conflict (diamond problem)
notes: A and B both have `default void show()`. If class C implements A, B **without overriding** show(), that is a **compile error**: 'inherits unrelated defaults' (verified).
Fix: override `show()` in C. To reuse one version, call **`A.super.show();`**.
Output of `new C().show()`: `Resolving conflict by overriding`, then `Default method from A`.
Related rule (not on the slide): a method inherited from a superclass beats an interface default ('class wins', verified).

items.title: Static methods in interfaces
notes: `interface Utility { static void displayMessage() {...} }` is a helper or utility method (Java 8).
Call it only as **`Utility.displayMessage()`**. It is **not inherited**: calling it via an implementing class name or an object is a compile error (verified).
It cannot be overridden.

items.title: Summary: default vs static vs abstract
notes: **Default**: add methods without breaking existing code. Can be overridden: **Yes**.
**Static**: utility or helper functions. Can be overridden: **No**.
**Abstract**: must be implemented by classes. Can be overridden: **Yes** (you implement it).

items.title: Traditional vs enhanced switch
notes: Traditional: `case MONDAY: num = 1; break;`. Forgetting `break` falls through to the next case.
Enhanced: `int num = switch (day) { case MONDAY -> 1; ... default -> 0; };`. The switch is an **expression** assigned directly, and it ends with **`};`**.
A switch *expression* must be **exhaustive**. Without `default` on an int or char it is a compile error. An enum switch that lists every constant needs no default (verified).

items.title: Arrow labels with multiple values
notes: `case 'A', 'B' -> 100;` puts **multiple labels in one case**, separated by commas.
`grade='B'` gives 100, `'C'` gives 75, anything else gives 50.
Arrow cases **never fall through**, so no break is needed (verified: arrow prints only `one `, colon style prints `one two def`).

items.title: yield in switch expressions
notes: Use a block body when you need statements: `case 'A' -> { System.out.println("Excellent"); yield 100; }`.
**`yield` returns the value from the block**. Not `return`, and not `break`.
For grade 'A' it prints `Excellent` and finalScore = 100 (verified).

items.title: Enhanced switch with an enum
notes: `case SATURDAY, SUNDAY -> "Relax"; default -> "Work";` so day = SUNDAY gives "Relax".
Case labels use the bare constant name (`SATURDAY`, not `Day.SATURDAY`).

items.title: Enhanced switch benefits
notes: **No fall-through** (eliminates common errors). **Expression support** (assign the result directly to a variable). **Concise and cleaner code**.

items.title: Version summary: 'Java 12+'
notes: Java 5: Generics, Collections enhancements, Enhanced for. Java 8: Lambdas, Streams, Default methods. **Java 12+: Enhanced switch**. Benefits: type safety, functional programming, concise syntax, fewer runtime errors.
Real history: the switch expression was a preview in Java 12/13 and became standard in **Java 14**. `yield` arrived in 13. Exam: answer 'Java 12+' as the slides say.
